title: Biotechnologies for climate resilience - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

The relentless expansion of agriculture is ravaging biodiversity and the climate. Biotech can help redesign food systems for sustainability.

No magic techno-fix is coming to save us from the climate emergency1. It must be addressed where it originates, in geopolitics, ethics, justice, evolutionary psychology and our extractivist relationship to nature. By default, though, after decades of political paralysis on climate, new technology has become essential to reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Energy, the highest-emitting economic sector, now has robust low-carbon alternatives like solar and wind energy, with more on the way. But food and agriculture, the second-highest-emitting sector, is a different story — long overlooked and critically lacking in climate solutions2. Food and agriculture is also the hub of biotech research for climate mitigation and adaptation, the subject of a special Focus in this issue. If deployed at scale, many emerging biotechnologies could help tackle the acute challenge facing agriculture in the coming decades: to raise yields faster than historical rates, slash emissions and keep land use from expanding3. This journal supports efforts to fight climate breakdown, food insecurity and ecocide by strengthening the climate resilience of food systems and reducing their land footprint.In the 2015 Paris Agreement, world governments agreed to limit global warming to 1.5–2 °C above the preindustrial baseline. Only a decade later, crossing 1.5 °C is inevitable within years4. GHG emissions, while flattening, are at a record high. New modeling projects 2.9 °C in 2100 under current policies. Last year, the German physics and meteorological societies jointly warned of even more dangerous possible futures: 4–5 °C by 2100 and 2–3 °C as soon as 2050. Whatever the precise dates and temperatures turn out to be, all these pathways are very fast on the timescales of evolutionary adaptation. All will amplify extreme weather, mass extinctions in the biosphere and the chances of crossing irreversible climate tipping points, risking “systems failures that unravel societies across the globe”5.Even at the time of the Paris Agreement, it was clear to some climate scientists that staying below 1.5 °C was unlikely6. Simulating these temperature ceilings in the models required vast removals of CO2 from the atmosphere using methods that did not exist at scale in the real world. The favored hypothetical methods involved using huge tracts of land to take up CO2 in plants — “typically, one to two times the area of India”6 — and then burn the biomass for energy, capture the released carbon and bury it, schemes that some described as “fairy tales”. The schemes also defied earlier research indicating that cumulative pressures on land use had pushed the planetary boundary of land-system change past its safe limit7.Land is a scarce and precious resource. Unchecked agricultural expansion is making it scarcer still. Agriculture has overtaken ~43% of Earth’s ice- and desert-free land8 and produces one-quarter of GHG emissions3. It is the single biggest driver of biodiversity loss and habitat destruction on land, just as fishing is for the oceans9. According to a World Resources Institute report, meeting projected food demand through 2050, assuming continued historical yield increases, will take 593 million more hectares of agricultural land beyond the 2010 level, a size approaching two Indias3. This ongoing land grab is on track to consume immense areas of remaining forests, savannas and grasslands, destroy much wildlife and biodiversity, and pump far too much carbon into the atmosphere3. We are eating2 and devouring10 the planet. To keep people fed through mid-century and emissions in line with 2 °C, the World Resources Institute provides 22 strategies to cut agricultural emissions by two-thirds (over 2010–2050) while increasing food production 56% and preventing net expansion of agricultural land3.Agriculture’s destructive impacts on the climate and biodiversity come not just from producing food but also from converting natural landscapes to cropland and pastureland, which are generally worse at storing carbon. Many putative climate biotechnologies depend on biomass, and therefore land. But life-cycle assessments (LCAs) to measure their climate impact typically underestimate the land-use contribution if the biomass is grown on existing agricultural land. To the contrary, exploiting such land just perpetuates the carbon-storage deficit, and if the biotech application displaces food production, more cropland is needed elsewhere. Land use has a high “carbon opportunity cost”11. Its centrality in carbon accounting makes it a simple test for identifying an effective climate biotechnology (Searchinger, this issue): will the technology reduce land use, or alternatively, will it reduce emissions without expanding land use?Biofuels, a biotech product supported by over 80 governments in the name of ‘renewable’ fuels, illustrate land’s high carbon cost and the reason for such a simple test. When carbon opportunity cost is factored in, biofuels are more damaging to the climate than are gasoline and diesel11. Compared with solar panels, they require at least 100-fold more land to produce the same energy and, compared with a solar-powered electric vehicle, at least 250-fold more land to drive the same distance (Searchinger, this issue). This means that the same quantity of mileage that the United States realizes from, say, 40 million acres of biofuel crops (after counting byproduct credits) could be supported by just approximately 160,000 acres of solar panels, leaving 39.8 million acres free for other uses — like growing food or reforestation to protect biodiversity and carbon storage.The land-use test also reveals potential winning biotechnologies, including crops engineered for high yields, reduced emissions or heat adaptation; and alternative proteins12, which, with wide uptake, “could do more to save global land than any other change” (Searchinger, this issue).Alternative proteins will save land if they can roll back the colossal acreage devoted to meat and milk production — the size of North and South America combined, or 77% of all agricultural land. Biotech produces alternative proteins through ‘cellular agriculture’. After 12,000 years of animal and plant domestication, cellular agriculture is domesticating animal, plant and bacterial cells for use in cell-culture systems such as precision fermentation and cultivated meat and seafood (Gassler et al., this issue). Because cells grow quickly, these methods can churn out food much faster than agriculture does. They can make meat and dairy products without animals, seafood products without fish, egg-white protein without chickens, and palm oil without plantations that spur deforestation. They can also improve food quality and safety and, because no animals are involved, avoid the pollution, animal cruelty and zoonotic disease risk of livestock farming.Cultivating cells in bioreactors usually relies on sugar feedstocks grown on farms. Still, a meta-LCA in preprint13 shows impressive decreases in land use (87–99%) for fermentation-derived dairy and egg proteins in the four LCAs that assessed it. In principle, gas fermentation in place of sugar feedstocks could save even more land. Solar Foods makes the high-protein biomass product Solein “from air” with bacteria that grow on CO2 and green hydrogen, which it produces through water electrolysis powered by renewable energy.Adapting agriculture to warming conditions is another major opportunity for climate biotech. Breeding timelines are falling thanks to a formidable biotech toolkit. Genomics, phenomics and enviromics, combined with AI to interpret big datasets, are speeding up selection of valuable mutations, while genome-editing methods can install them precisely and rapidly. Seed companies are boosting climate resilience by fine-tuning diverse traits like flowering time, growing-season time, light interception and height (Sheridan, this issue). But resistance to heat and drought tend to be polygenic, arising from hard-to-identify small changes in many genes. The full germplasm of domesticated crop varieties and their wild relatives is thought to harbor a rich genetic reservoir for enhancing such traits, but whether breeding programs can keep up with the rate of global warming remains to be seen.Similar questions complicate the outlook for agricultural yields. Higher-than-historical yields are needed to close the food gap by midcentury3, and high yields can lower emissions by sparing agricultural land. But yield gains from breeding, currently 1–2% per year at best, could be outpaced by heat waves, droughts, and associated diseases and insects. In addition to optimizing the best seeds, there is considerable room to improve yields by raising low- and average-yielding fields toward the performance of top-yielding fields. Climate-induced declines in yield affect breadbaskets and subsistence economies alike14. But lower-income, climate-vulnerable countries are most at risk of food shortages and malnutrition, and also least responsible for climate change.At least 77 biotechnologies for agricultural sustainability are in the pipeline (Mishra et al., this issue). Some aim to lower the GHG emissions of crops, fertilizers and livestock. Low-methane rice, demonstrated in several elite rice lines, is poised for translation to the thousands of cultivars planted worldwide (Jin et al., this issue). Research on reducing emissions from nitrogen fertilizers is seeking to harness nature’s solutions for microbial nitrogen fixation (Haskett et al., this issue) and nitrification inhibition and to perennialize annual crops.Beyond agriculture, biotech is being explored for coral reef protection, cement manufacturing, enhanced rock weathering and other climate applications. In chemical manufacturing, as with biofuels, the claim that fermentation-derived chemicals are a green solution to petrochemicals underestimates the climate cost of relying on biomass (Nielsen et al., this issue). One area where biotech could have profound impact is in combating mosquito-borne diseases like malaria and dengue, whose spread is partly climate dependent (Christophides & Alphey, this issue). Biotech tools to suppress mosquitoes are starting to be deployed in communities. Gene drives, in particular, promise long-lasting efficacy that existing eradication methods lack.World-changing technologies require massive investment, proactive policy, supportive publics and enlightened regulators. Solar and wind met 99% of new global electricity (not energy) demand last year and are driving the clean energy transition. In two decades, they went from providing just 0.74% of global electricity to 17% in 2025, propelled by investments of more than $5 trillion. No climate biotechnology will succeed without huge injections of capital. Globally, climate financing for agriculture in 2024 was only $8.9 billion, compared with $950 billion for energy. Yet this spending gap hints at a steep potential upside for agricultural solutions with sufficient investment.Sustained engagement with the public and regulators is crucial. Alternative proteins provide a lesson in how progress can be hindered. In the United States, five cultivated meat products have gained approval, and around two dozen precision-fermented non-enzyme proteins, primarily dairy whey, egg and sweet proteins, have Generally Recognized as Safe clearance. But openness to innovation at the federal level hasn’t stopped eight states from banning or restricting cultivated meat. In the European Union, an endless debate about food labels — do consumers understand that a ‘veggie burger’ isn’t meat? — has mired alternative proteins in bureaucratic oversight. The approval pathway there for novel foods is so gridlocked that no precision-fermented protein or cultivated meat product has received market authorization.The landscape of expert views on climate shows that averting the worst impacts requires a combination of rapid, deep decarbonization across the economy, adaptation and nature-based solutions. What exactly the Earth’s irreversible climate tipping points are, and how they behave over time, are hard to identify before it’s too late to stop them. A ‘social tipping point’ to restore the global community to safe planetary boundaries cannot come soon enough.
